title: From God to the Atom and Back
subtitle: A travelogue from the frontier of fundamental physics

blocks.html: When I was a little boy, my father told me that reality is basically made up of little bits of stuff pushing each other around by the fundamental forces. I learned about how protons, neutrons, and electrons combine to form atoms; that the particle of light is the photon—the strange, virtually massless keeper of the cosmic speed limit. Electrons orbit atomic nuclei, atoms are bonded into crystals and molecules, and small molecules are bonded and folded into larger ones. Gravity keeps us on the ground and the Earth and Moon in their orbits. Like most kids, my exposure to this fundamental ontology was lightweight at least until high school. Atoms and molecules came up in elementary school science class; I recall a book about black holes for young readers; I enjoyed the Earth and Space museum, where the Timeline of the Universe walkway wrapped its chronicle from the Big Bang up around the planetarium sphere. Through my dad (a physician) and the wider culture, I had been introduced to the long tradition of materialist reductionism often identified with Democritus, whom Aristotle famously credited with the theory of the atom.

The Atomists are known for proposing the existence of the atom. But if we trace more closely the contours of their thought, the word “atom” enters in an adjectival role to illuminate a prior inquiry about the quality of ordinary substances. Are things infinitely divisible? That is: if you had fine enough instruments, could you continue to divide a quantity of water or a length of spider silk in half indefinitely? The same problem concerning distance and time, today commonly associated with Xeno, was familiar to the Atomists, who answered No. Rather, there must exist a smallest possible “uncuttable” unit (ἄτομον) of each substance.

Democritus theorized that atoms varied in shape, size, and motion and moved through a void, combining to form all observable phenomena. This idea was entirely philosophical, as it was based on reasoning rather than empirical evidence. When I first learned about Plato, it was not in science class.
